newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul expects breakthrough over defector in China.
newsitem.headline: Seoul expects breakthrough over defector in China.

text.p: South Korea said on Monday it expected a breakthrough this week in talks with China aimed at securing passage out of Beijing of North Korea's top ideologue.
Hwang Jang-yop has been holed up in a South Korean diplomatic mission in Beijing since seeking aslyum there on February 12.

China has agonised over Hwang's fate, torn between an old socialist comrade and a new capitalist friend. Weeks of talks, interrupted by the death of paramount Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, have failed to reach agreement.
"I don't expect Hwang to leave Beijing this week but details of his departure will be discussed this week and could be worked out," said one foreign ministry official, who declined to be identified.
"Unlike previous discussions, talks this week will deal with Hwang's future in a package, including the method and the timing of his departure. A breakthrough is probable," he said.
North Korea initially accused South Korea of kidnapping Hwang, then said if he really had defected he was a renegade and would be dismissed.
South Korean foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said he believed Beijing would not send Hwang home.
"I understand both sides have formed a common stand that a solution must be found as soon as possible," Lee told Reuters. "I believe China has ruled out sending him back to North Korea."
Lee said South Korea wanted to send Hwang directly to Seoul but would not rule out bringing him via a third country.
Hwang, chief architect of Pyongyang's ruling ideology of Juche, or self-reliance, is the highest North Korean official to flee the communist country.
China, which fought on North Korea's side during the 1950-53 Korean war, established diplomatic relations with South Korea only in 1992.

Separately, five North Korean soldiers crossed into the southern portion of a border buffer zone on Monday in violation of the armistice agreement that ended hostilities in the Korean conflict, a U.S. military spokesman said.
Jim Coles said the crossing took place before dawn "and we watched them for about one and a half hours".
"While their presence in the area is a violation of the armistice agreement, they did not do anything provocative. It's rugged territory up there and it's easy to miss the line markers," Coles said.
The armed soldiers crossed a demarcation line through the four-km (2.5 mile) deep Demilitarised Zone, which bisects the Korean peninsula.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea and helps monitor the ceasefire.
A Seoul defence ministry official said such incursions were not unusual. "We are not very concerned," he said.
Last April scores of North Korean troops carrying heavy weapons crossed the demarcation line on three occasions within the sensitive border crossing area of Panmunjom, sparking security concerns.
Those violations followed a North Korean announcement it would no longer respect the terms of the armistice.
Tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang have been heightened since the defection of Hwang and the murder in South Korea last month of an earlier North Korean defector.
Despite tensions, North Korean officials attended a briefing by officials from South Korea and the United States on proposed four-way peace talks, also involving China.
The New York briefing was intended to lure Pyongyang into talks to secure a peace agreement to replace the truce.
